deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematical derivation. It is a heavily corrected German prose draft of an expert report (Gutachten) to the Royal Hanoverian government. The context comes from the previous and next pages: 'Die Unterzeichneten', the 'hohe Rescripte', and the cooperation of the 'Königliche Hannoversche Regierung' with the 'angeregte Unternehmen'. The undertaking is almost certainly J. J. Baeyer's proposal of 1861/62 for a Central European arc measurement (Mitteleuropäische Gradmessung). Riemann was evidently one of the Göttingen co-authors.

The argument, restated:

(1) Recent reductions of arc measurements (an English one and another; the second word is illegible, possibly 'russischen' or 'ostindischen') no longer simply average discrepancies by least squares. The draft says the earlier least-squares treatment shows the accuracy of the results in a false light.

(2) These newer treatments were prompted by the results of Gauss's Hanoverian arc measurement. There the differences between geodetic and astronomical latitude differences were about 5" for Göttingen–Altona and 16" for Altona and a second station (reading of the name uncertain). Such differences cannot come mainly from measuring errors. For by far the greatest part they must be due to local deflections of the vertical (Lothabweichungen). Riemann adds that, contrary to a remark in a cited publication (citation left blank), such deflections are not to be expected only near very large mountains.

(3) In one work (very probably the British Ordnance Survey reduction, or Pratt's Himalaya computations), the attraction of the masses rising above sea level was computed for many stations. The computed deflections were then subtracted from the observed plumb-line directions. Riemann's verdict: in this way the true local deflections cannot be found, because invisible density anomalies are ignored. This is the issue made famous by Pratt (1855) and Airy's isostasy hypothesis (1855).

(4) His proposal: local deflections could be found far more completely from gravity values at a sufficient number of points. Differences of gravity would be measured by comparative pendulum observations, with time compared over the electric telegraph. This is the method Airy used in his Harton colliery determination of the mean density of the Earth (1854). It is accurate enough for the purpose and could perhaps be simplified.

(5) English experience suggested that only masses within a limited distance (number of miles left blank) matter. So the survey need cover only a limited area, and could be carried out for the Hanoverian arc alone if supplemented by pendulum observations. Part of the pendulum apparatus is said to exist already.

The physical idea behind this, stated in modern terms by me: horizontal gradients of the disturbing potential T give the deflection of the vertical, roughly xi = -(1/(g r)) dT/dphi. T in turn can be determined from gravity anomalies, as in Stokes 1849 and Vening Meinesz 1928. The draft states only the qualitative idea, with no formula.
errors: The statement that least-squares treatment of the Hanoverian arc 'proved' the discrepancies arise mostly from plumb-line deflections is an interpretive claim, consistent with Gauss's own conclusion (1828).
The 16" figure and the name of the second station (transcribed 'Seeberg') cannot be verified from the image; it is uncertain.

results.what: Discrepancies between astronomical and geodetic latitude differences in Gauss's Hanoverian arc are attributed mainly to local deflections of the vertical, not measuring error.
results.modern_name: deflection of the vertical / astrogeodetic discrepancy

results.what: Criticism that computing the attraction of visible topography does not give the true local deflections.
Proposal to determine local plumb-line deflections from relative gravity (pendulum) measurements, with time transfer by electric telegraph, over a limited region around the stations.
results.modern_name: gravimetric determination of deflections of the vertical (Stokes / Vening Meinesz approach); relative gravimetry with telegraphic time comparison
results.usually_credited_to: Stokes 1849 (theory), Vening Meinesz 1928 (formula); Airy 1854 (telegraph pendulum comparison); Helmert later systematized it

deep.surprise_reason: Riemann's participation in Göttingen reports on Baeyer's arc measurement project is a minor documented biographical fact. The page is non-mathematical administrative-scientific prose. The suggestion to use pendulum gravimetry for deflections is sensible and not new in principle (Stokes 1849), though an explicit practical proposal in 1861/62 is a modest point of interest.

checkable.asserts: A 5 arcsecond discrepancy in latitude corresponds to about 154 m on the Earth's surface.
A 16 arcsecond discrepancy corresponds to about 494 m.

transcription_corrections: 'der englischen und russischen' — the second adjective is uncertain; it may be 'ostindischen', referring to Pratt and the Indian arc.

'Die frühere Methode der kleinsten Quadrate, welche aber die Genauigkeit ... in falschem Lichte zeigt' — probably 'Die früheren, nach der Methode der kleinsten Quadrate geführten Rechnungen ... lieferten den Beweis'; the syntax of the transcription is garbled.
'Altona und Seeberg' — the station name is doubtful in the image.
The stray '57' at the right margin is the folio number, not text.
'Bei einzelnen[?] sich an sämmtlichen Stationen' — likely 'Es ergaben sich an sämmtlichen Stationen ...'; uncertain.
